`alloca()` should really only be used for a "handful" of elements (like, <20 as an arbitrary number), not 100s or 1000s. If we really have that many elements, then I absolutely think that allocating the arrays on the heap is the right way to go.

However, this is a pretty general method - it doesn't seem like it _usually_ has this many elements? If it has much fewer elements in most cases then always allocating on the heap would likely be detrimental for performance. Maybe it could switch to heap allocation over a certain threshold?

I can push a PR that swaps the source of the allocation based on the elements count. It's likely the selected limit will have to be arbitrary given there's no reliable mechanism to detect the stack limit across platforms.

> It's likely the selected limit will have to be arbitrary given there's no reliable mechanism to detect the stack limit across platforms.

Personally, I think this is fine. Regardless of the platform's stack limit, we really shouldn't be using `alloca()` for things that are boundless - it should always be for something where we have an idea that the upper limit is somewhat reasonable.

For example, we use `alloca()` in GDExtension and `JavaClassWrapper` for lists of method arguments when marshalling data across the Godot <-> GDExtension boundary or the C++ <-> Java boundary. A method will only have so many arguments - you can't end up with 100s or 1000s.

Whereas a developer in Godot could connect to a signal 100 times, because we don't enforce any sort of limit on that. So, we either need to start enforcing some limit on the number of connections, or have a code path that doesn't use `alloca()` when we're over some "reasonable" number.

> Whereas a developer in Godot could connect to a signal 100 times, because we don't enforce any sort of limit on that. So, we either need to start enforcing some limit on the number of connections, or have a code path that doesn't use `alloca()` when we're over some "reasonable" number.

It's tricky because it's definitely a performance concern when there are that many connections, so it's likely the choice here was made because there was no expectation to have this sort of volume. Whether that is a valid expectation or short-sightedness, that's a matter of hindsight :P

As I mentioned on rocketchat, it's worth discussing whether we should rethink the action map tab. This was my first major implementation for the editor UI. There are two things in particular that we should consider:
- I might be applying themes wrong here, we really need someone from the editor team to take a look and see whether we're not doing something wrong. We might be looking at the flow on effects from me doing something dumb and fighting symptoms instead of solving the core issue
- The way Godot does tabs is... I don't think it was ever meant for the use case I'm applying. We're loading in every tab whether visible or not. It makes much more sense to populate the UI for a tab when we switch to that. That said, Godots Undo/Redo system seems to be tied into the UI surviving, that is another area the action map interface probably could use a cleanup.
